passage: Tuesday night. Pankaj laughed at Rohit's joke about the tea seller today. Last year he walked out of a room when someone did that. Everyone laughed: Tanya, Rohit, the two new boys from Pankaj's lab group. I did not, and Tanya looked at me, then looked away. Pankaj caught my eye and stopped laughing a second too late. I do not want to say anything in front of everyone. Tomorrow I will ask him for chai, just us, and say what I noticed, not that he is wrong. Maybe there is a reason. Maybe I am the one who has it wrong. — Shalini

qa.q: Whose joke did Pankaj laugh at?
qa.a: Pankaj laughed at Rohit's joke about the tea seller.

qa.q: What is Shalini worried about, and why does Shalini hold back from speaking in front of everyone?
qa.a: Shalini is worried and unsure: a change in Pankaj was noticed, but Shalini does not want to confront anyone publicly and allows that there may be a reason.

qa.q: What choice does Shalini make about how to raise the change with Pankaj?
qa.a: Shalini plans a private chai with Pankaj, saying what was noticed rather than saying Pankaj is wrong, which leaves room for an explanation.

qa.q: What might Pankaj be feeling when catching Shalini's eye and stopping the laugh a second too late?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel caught between fitting in and old values; stopping late suggests discomfort or guilt at what everyone was laughing at.

grounding: A person notices someone laughing at jokes they used to dislike and chooses a private, kind check-in over public teasing.

passage:
Anirban: free for a walk after class? nothing serious
Rafiq: sure why
Anirban: you laughed at Sahil's joke about Dev's accent today
Anirban: not like you. that's all
Rafiq: everyone was laughing 🤔
Anirban: yeah I saw. Tanmay didn't laugh and I didn't. no lecture, I just noticed
Rafiq: ...ok. honestly I'm tired of being the odd one in that group
Anirban: you're not odd to me
Anirban: I just miss talking about the stuff we used to
Anirban: chai tomorrow? you can tell me or not, your call

qa.q: Whose accent was the joke about?

qa.q: Why does Rafiq say "honestly I'm tired of being the odd one in that group"?

qa.q: What choice by Anirban made it easy for Rafiq to answer honestly?
qa.a: Anirban asked privately, said "no lecture", named what was noticed and left it to Rafiq whether to explain.

qa.q: What might Anirban be feeling when writing "I just miss talking about the stuff we used to"?
qa.a: Anirban probably feels a little sad and lonely for the old friendship, and cares enough to reach out privately instead of lecturing.

grounding: A person notices someone laughing at jokes they used to dislike and chooses a private, kind check-in over public teasing.

passage: At the cooperative bank in the small town, the shutters came down at four, but the ledgers stayed open till eight. Asif had finished the day's entries by half past four. He opened the ledger again and checked pages he had already checked. Kavitha, the senior clerk, was still tapping at her calculator, and Prakash, the peon, sipped his third tea. Nobody looked at the clock. Asif thought of the 5.45 bus he was missing yet again. "If I leave first, they will think I do not care," he told himself, and took the last auto home at nine.

qa.q: When had Asif finished the day's entries?
qa.a: Asif had finished the day's entries by half past four.

qa.q: Why does Asif stay at the bank when the work is done?
qa.a: Asif fears looking less committed if he leaves first, so he is anxious about being judged; the worry is about how others see him, not about the ledgers.

qa.q: What small step could Asif take to test whether the late evenings are really needed?
qa.a: Asif could ask Kavitha which task truly needs the evening hours, or leave on time one day with a friendly word.

qa.q: What might Kavitha be thinking while she taps at the calculator long after closing?
qa.a: Kavitha may have real work left, or may be following the same custom without asking; nothing in the scene shows that anyone has questioned it.

grounding: A young professional stays late because everyone does, though the work is done, and fears seeming less committed.

passage: By four o'clock Ines had sent the report, but in the Lisbon open-plan office jackets still hung over chairs like little flags. Emil ate a sandwich at his desk and murmured, "One more thing," though his screen was blank. Marta, the team head, was on a long call with her door open. At five Tomas quietly packed his bag and left, and two people glanced at his empty chair. Ines opened an old spreadsheet and scrolled without reading. She wondered whether anyone truly needed her at seven, and whether anyone would say so if she asked.

qa.q: What hung over the chairs in the Lisbon office?
qa.a: Jackets hung over the chairs like little flags.

qa.q: What is Ines worried about while scrolling the old spreadsheet?
qa.a: Ines worries about looking less committed than the others, and doubts whether staying is needed at all.

qa.q: What could Ines ask or try instead of scrolling through an old spreadsheet?
qa.a: Ines could ask Marta which work really needs evening hours, or leave on time once and see what actually happens.

qa.q: How might Tomas have felt when leaving at five while two people glanced at his chair?
qa.a: Tomas may have felt a little self-conscious but settled enough to go; packing quietly and leaving suggests he had decided the work was done.

grounding: A young professional stays late because everyone does though the work is done, and rarely asks whether the norm serves anyone.

passage: Come, sit, and I will tell you what my first office taught me. I was twenty-four then, and the nameplate said Swati Rao. A woman called Deepika sat at the next desk. She greeted the guard by name every morning and brought sweets on birthdays. But when the lunch table started picking apart a colleague's marriage, Deepika said lightly, "I will pass, tell me when the food comes," and went on eating. No speech, no frown. Two others went quiet too, though Mahesh kept talking a little. Nobody stopped inviting her. The following week I tried her line myself, and my voice shook only a little.

qa.q: What did Deepika say when the lunch table started picking apart a colleague's marriage?
qa.a: Deepika said lightly, "I will pass, tell me when the food comes," and went on eating.

qa.q: What might Deepika have been feeling while she declined with no speech and no frown?
qa.a: Deepika seems calm and unbothered, without needing to win or condemn anyone; going on eating suggests she was comfortable dissenting.

qa.q: What did Swati take from Deepika that helped when trying it the next week?
qa.a: Swati used Deepika's light line and did not lecture anyone, which made saying no small enough to try even with a shaky voice.

qa.q: How might it have felt for Deepika when the table went quiet after "I will pass"?
qa.a: Deepika may have felt a small flicker of worry about the silence, but the daily invitations that followed show the group accepted it.

grounding: A mature young adult keeps courtesy but politely declines gossip, dissenting calmly without needing to win, told as an elder's memory.

passage: Fifteen minutes before the auditors arrived, the pantry was crowded and the lights kept flickering. Kunal filled tea cups for the visitors, the way he always did, thanking the cleaner as he passed. Yamini, stirring sugar, lowered her voice: "Did you hear why Rekha is on leave? Apparently..." Two people leaned in. A third, Vikram, studied the biscuit tin. Kunal kept pouring. "I would rather not talk about Rekha," he said mildly. "Can we check the cash register figures before they come?" Yamini shrugged and laughed, "Fine, boss." The lights flickered again, and Kunal carried the tray out first.

qa.q: How many minutes remained before the auditors arrived?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes remained before the auditors arrived.

qa.q: Why does Kunal keep pouring tea and answer so mildly when Yamini starts gossiping?
qa.a: Kunal wants to decline the gossip without a fight; the mild tone and the change of topic suggest calm, not a wish to condemn Yamini.

qa.q: What made Kunal's refusal easy for the group to accept?
qa.a: Kunal offered a useful alternative, checking the cash register figures, and did not criticise Yamini, so nobody had to lose face.

qa.q: What might Vikram be feeling while studying the biscuit tin during the gossip?
qa.a: Vikram may feel uncomfortable, unwilling to join in but also unwilling to speak up, so looking away is a way of staying out of it.

grounding: A young adult follows courtesy norms such as serving tea but politely declines gossip, without needing to win or condemn.

passage: In a Cape Town park, Vera called, "Amara, come to me!" in a bright sing-song, and Amara toddled back, laughing. Then at the pond's edge Vera's voice flattened: "Amara. Stop." Amara froze, one foot in the air, and looked up at Vera's face. At the slide, Nico's minder said "Nico" in a bored voice, and Nico climbed on. A baby in a pram watched them all.

qa.q: What did Vera say at the pond's edge?
qa.a: Vera said, "Amara. Stop."

qa.q: How does Amara seem to feel when Vera's voice flattens at the pond?
qa.a: Amara seems startled and unsure, freezing mid-step and looking up at Vera's face to read the flat tone.

qa.q: What could Vera do to keep Amara safe near the pond without frightening Amara?
qa.a: Vera could walk over, crouch down and use a warm but firm voice, so the signal is clear without being alarming.

qa.q: What might the bored tone mean for Nico, who kept climbing?
qa.a: A bored tone carries little urgency, so Nico feels free to go on; the same word from a different face gave a very different signal.

grounding: A toddler stops or goes on according to a caregiver's face and tone, obeying the emotional signal more than the words.

passage: From my balcony I watch the courtyard most evenings. Hansa, about two, was touching the gate latch while her father Nilesh chatted with two other parents. He said "No, Hansa" laughing, and she grinned and touched it again. A minute later he said the same words in a flat, firm voice without turning round, and she snatched her hand away and stood still, lip trembling. I cannot say what she understood. Nilesh lifted her and rubbed her back.

qa.q: What did Nilesh say when Hansa touched the latch?
qa.a: Nilesh said "No, Hansa" laughing, and later said the same words in a flat, firm voice.

qa.q: What might Hansa be feeling when the flat voice comes and her lip trembles?
qa.a: Hansa may feel startled or worried; the trembling lip suggests a reaction to the tone, though the neighbour cannot be sure what Hansa understood.

qa.q: What could Nilesh try next time when Hansa touches the latch?
qa.a: Nilesh could walk over, take Hansa's hand and speak in the same calm voice as the first time, so tone and words match.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have meant by the second "No, Hansa" said without turning round?
qa.a: Nilesh may have been worried about little fingers at the latch, or busy talking, and not noticed the tone had changed; the neighbour cannot tell.

grounding: A toddler responds to a caregiver's tone rather than words, seen by an observer who cannot be sure of the child's inner state.

passage: "Ankita! Shoes! Now!" Papa's voice cracked like a whip. Ankita dropped her crayon and ran, and put her shoes on the wrong feet. "Good girl," said Papa. "See how fast she listens, Amma." "Look at her hands, Pankaj," said Dadi quietly. "They are shaking." "She is only being quick." "She is being careful. That is not the same." Ankita stood very still, watching Papa's face, waiting to see if she had done it right.

qa.q: What did Ankita do with her shoes?
qa.a: Ankita put her shoes on the wrong feet.

qa.q: What is Ankita feeling as she stands still watching Papa's face?
qa.a: Ankita feels anxious, waiting to learn whether she has avoided disapproval; the shaking hands and stillness show fear behind the quick obedience.

qa.q: What could Papa try the next time shoes are needed?
qa.a: Papa could call Ankita in an ordinary voice, walk over and help with the shoes, so listening comes from trust rather than fear.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Ankita's quick obedience?
qa.a: Dadi sees the shaking hands as carefulness born of worry, not good discipline, and says being quick and being careful are not the same.

grounding: A young child obeys quickly when an adult's voice turns sharp, looking like discipline while the inner state is anxiety.

passage: Observation note, KG2. When the room got noisy, the substitute teacher raised her voice: "Tidy up, now!" Lakshmi was the first up, packing blocks with wide eyes and a tight mouth, hardly looking at anyone. The other children finished slowly, chatting, and Manav kept building. At the end Lakshmi asked me quietly, "Am I in trouble?" I said no, and that the voice had been loud because the room was noisy. I plan to tell her parents at pickup that she seems to tidy up out of fear, and I will use a calm tone in class. — Karthik Sir

qa.q: Who was the first to pack away the blocks?
qa.a: Lakshmi was the first up, packing the blocks.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi ask "Am I in trouble?" after tidying up so quickly?
qa.a: Lakshmi feared disapproval; the wide eyes and tight mouth show anxiety behind the fast tidying.

qa.q: What did Karthik Sir plan to do about it?
qa.a: Karthik Sir planned to tell Lakshmi's parents at pickup that she seems to tidy up out of fear, and to use a calm tone in class.

qa.q: How might Manav have experienced the same loud voice, compared with Lakshmi?
qa.a: Manav kept building, so the voice seems to have carried less alarm for Manav; the same sound meant different things to different children.

grounding: A young child obeys quickly when an adult's voice turns sharp, and a teacher's note shows the anxiety behind the good behaviour.

passage: In the small-town school, Master-ji tapped his cane. "Hrithik, take Jomon's slate and lock it in the almirah. He talks too much." Hrithik stood up at once. Jomon's face crumpled, but Hrithik did not look at him. Meena at the back frowned, and two boys stared at the floor. Hrithik's stomach felt odd, as if a stone had settled there. But Master-ji had said it, and Master-ji was never wrong. He put the slate in the almirah and went back to his seat, holding the key very carefully.

qa.q: What did Master-ji tell Hrithik to do with Jomon's slate?
qa.a: Master-ji told Hrithik to take Jomon's slate and lock it in the almirah.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik obey even though Hrithik's stomach feels odd?
qa.a: Hrithik trusts Master-ji and believes Master-ji is never wrong; the stone-like feeling suggests an uneasy sense that the order may be unfair.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try at the moment the order is given?
qa.a: Hrithik could ask politely why, or say that Jomon needs the slate for the lesson, separating respect for the teacher from agreeing with every order.

qa.q: How might Jomon experience the order?
qa.a: Jomon's crumpled face suggests hurt and humiliation, made sharper by Hrithik taking the slate without looking at Jomon.

grounding: A child does what a teacher says only because of who said it, and cannot yet separate a fair rule from an unfair order.

passage: In a Toronto school library, Mr Grant told Class 4, "Nobody sits on the red carpet." The carpet was empty and soft. Yara raised her hand. "Why not, sir?" "Because I said so." Yara shrugged and sat on a chair. Fatima had a tired leg and looked longingly at the carpet, but she stood by the shelf for the whole story hour, reading spines. Two other children leaned against the wall. When the bell rang, Fatima's leg ached, but she said nothing, and neither did anyone else.

qa.q: Where did Fatima stand during story hour?
qa.a: Fatima stood by the shelf for the whole story hour, reading spines.

qa.q: Why does Fatima stand by the shelf despite a tired leg?
qa.a: Fatima follows the rule simply because the teacher said it and feels shy about asking; trust in adults is there, but the line between a fair rule and an unexplained one is not yet clear.

qa.q: What could Fatima do next time when a rule seems pointless and a leg is tired?
qa.a: Fatima could ask politely as Yara did, or say the leg is tired and ask whether sitting on a chair is allowed.

qa.q: What might Yara have been thinking when asking "Why not, sir?" and hearing "Because I said so"?
qa.a: Yara wanted a reason and was not convinced; shrugging and sitting on a chair suggests Yara accepted the rule without pretending it had been explained.

grounding: A child obeys a teacher's order without understanding it, showing healthy trust that has not yet learned to tell fair rules from unfair ones.

passage: I was on the compound wall eating peanuts when it happened. Yash, from Class 8, stood with two other big boys near the water tank. Little Santosh from Class 5 held a piece of a broken flowerpot and looked as if he might cry. "Just bury it under the bush and say nothing," said Yash. "Or you will be the one who broke it." Santosh looked at the bush, then at the staff room, then at the ground. The other two big boys watched. I could not tell what Santosh would do; his hand shook. After the bell I told our class teacher what I had seen, and she went to the tank straight away.

qa.q: Where did Yash tell Santosh to bury the piece of flowerpot?
qa.a: Yash told Santosh to bury it under the bush and say nothing.

qa.q: What might Santosh be feeling as looking from the bush to the staff room to the ground?
qa.a: Santosh seems torn and frightened: pulled to obey an older boy, yet with a sinking sense that hiding the piece is wrong.

qa.q: What choice by the narrator helped after the bell?
qa.a: The narrator told the class teacher what had been seen, and the teacher went to the water tank straight away.

qa.q: Why might the two other big boys stay silent while Yash speaks?
qa.a: They may fear that speaking against Yash would make them the next target, or may be following along to belong; the passage shows only that they watch.

grounding: A child is told by an older student to hide something and keep a secret, feeling the pull between obedience and a sense of wrongness.

passage: Monday. On the school bus Dhruv from Class 8 leaned over. "Put Eshaan's bottle in your bag, Alka. Do not tell." Alka laughed as if it were a joke, then did it. Her stomach sank. Tuesday. Eshaan searched under every seat with pink eyes, and Alka could not swallow her lunch. Dhruv winked at her. Wednesday. In the corridor Alka gave the bottle back and told the class teacher what Dhruv had said. The teacher sat beside her, said she had done the right thing and it was not her fault, and took Dhruv and Eshaan to the head that same afternoon.

qa.q: What did Dhruv tell Alka to put in her bag?
qa.a: Dhruv told Alka to put Eshaan's bottle in her bag and not tell.

qa.q: How did Alka feel on Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: Alka felt guilty and uneasy: a sinking stomach and not being able to swallow lunch show the pull between obeying an older boy and knowing it was wrong.

qa.q: What turning point helped on Wednesday?
qa.a: Alka gave the bottle back and told the class teacher, who stayed with Alka, said it was not Alka's fault, and took the matter to the head that afternoon.

qa.q: What might Tuesday have been like for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan searched under every seat with pink eyes, which suggests worry and upset over the missing bottle, and no idea who could be responsible.

grounding: A child is told by an older student to hide something and keep quiet, feeling a stomach-sinking wrongness across three days.

passage: At the Class 10 assembly in a Mumbai school, the vice principal announced a new rule: no talking in the library at any time, including the project room. Sabina raised her hand. "Ma'am, who decided this, and what is it for? Group projects need talking." A murmur ran along the row. "Rules are rules, Sabina." Jyoti shrank in her seat and pulled at Sabina's sleeve; Rahul gave a thumbs-up under his desk. Sabina stayed standing. "I am not saying we should break it. I want to know why." The vice principal paused. "Meet me at lunch." Sabina's knees shook as she sat down.

qa.q: What new rule did the vice principal announce?
qa.a: The vice principal announced no talking in the library at any time, including the project room.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when pulling at Sabina's sleeve?
qa.a: Jyoti was anxious, fearing trouble for Sabina and perhaps for the row; the tug shows a wish for Sabina to sit down.

qa.q: What choice by Sabina kept the question respectful?
qa.a: Sabina said she was not saying to break the rule and only wanted to know why, which separated testing a rule from defiance.

qa.q: How might the vice principal see Sabina's question?
qa.a: The vice principal may first read it as defiance, given "Rules are rules", but the pause and the invitation to meet at lunch suggest some openness.

grounding: A teenager begins asking why a rule exists and who made it, which looks like defiance to adults expecting quick compliance.

passage: "Phones go off at ten," said Papa, tapping the table. "Why ten, Papa? Who decided?" asked Aparna. "I did." "But why not eleven? Riya's parents say eleven." "Aparna, do not compare." "I am not being rude. I just want to know the reason." Mummy looked up from her plate, and little Ronit, with his spoon halfway to his mouth, went very still. Papa sighed. "Sleep. School." "Then can I show you my timetable on Sunday and we decide together?" Papa was quiet. "Anirban, let her show you," said Mummy. Papa nodded slowly. "Show me on Sunday."

qa.q: What time did Papa say the phones go off?
qa.a: Papa said the phones go off at ten.

qa.q: How does Aparna feel about the ten o'clock rule, and what shows it?
qa.a: Aparna feels curious and a little frustrated, pressing “why ten” and “who decided” because she wants the reason, not to be rude.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna make that turned the argument into a talk?
qa.a: Aparna offered to show her timetable on Sunday and decide together, which gave Papa a way to say yes without losing authority.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ronit at the table while Aparna and Papa argue?
qa.a: Ronit went very still, which suggests tension and worry about the argument getting bigger.

grounding: A teenager asks why a rule exists and who made it, healthy testing that can look like defiance to a parent expecting quick compliance.

subtype: Teacher or coach crossing a line [Receiver]
passage: Rain hammered the hockey field, and the final was ten minutes from full time, tied. In the huddle Coach Mridul murmured, "Their striker is the danger. When I nod, foul her hard. The umpire cannot see in this rain." Sabina felt the cold go through her. Keya and Rina stared at their sticks. Nobody spoke. Sabina had always respected Coach Mridul, and refusing him felt unthinkable. When the nod came, she froze and did nothing. The whistle blew at a draw. That evening she went to the PE teacher, Ms Dsouza, and told her everything. Ms Dsouza sat with her, said it was not her fault, and took it to the principal before dark.

qa.q: Who spoke to the team in the huddle?
qa.a: Coach Mridul spoke in the huddle.

qa.q: Why did Sabina freeze when the nod came?
qa.a: Sabina respected Coach Mridul and feared him, so refusing felt unthinkable, but doing it felt wrong; respect and fear were mixed together.

qa.q: What turning point that evening helped Sabina?
qa.a: Sabina told the PE teacher Ms Dsouza everything, and Ms Dsouza stayed with Sabina, said it was not Sabina's fault, and took it to the principal before dark.

qa.q: How might Keya and Rina have felt in the huddle?
qa.a: Staring at their sticks suggests discomfort and unease, perhaps fear of the coach; since nobody spoke, each may have thought the others agreed.

grounding: A student is pressured by a coach to do something that feels wrong, with respect and fear mixed, and freezes rather than complying.

subtype: Teacher or coach crossing a line [Receiver]
passage: At a coaching class in Pune, Saurabh Sir tapped an answer key on the desk. "Copy this, Urmila. Sell it to the others before Friday's test, twenty rupees each, and I will see that your marks go up." Three students kept their heads down over their notebooks. Urmila felt her throat close. She admired Saurabh Sir; he had explained fractions so clearly. She took the paper and said nothing. That night she could not eat, and finally showed it to her mother. Her mother read it, held her hand, said it was not Urmila's fault, and rang the class head and the school principal that same evening. The principal called back before bedtime to say it was being looked into.

qa.q: How much did Saurabh Sir say each copy should sell for?
qa.a: Saurabh Sir said twenty rupees each.

qa.q: Why does Urmila take the paper and say nothing?
qa.a: Urmila admires Saurabh Sir and is frightened of refusing him, so her throat closes; respect and fear stop her from saying no, though she knows something is wrong.

qa.q: What helped Urmila after that night?
qa.a: Showing the paper to her mother helped: her mother listened, said it was not Urmila's fault, and rang the class head and the principal the same evening.

qa.q: How might the three students with their heads down have felt?
qa.a: They may be afraid of being noticed or chosen, or unsure what to do; keeping their heads down suggests they want to stay out of it.

grounding: A student is pressured by a tutor to do something that feels wrong, with respect and fear mixed, and a parent responds the same day.

passage: In a small-town school, Gautam Sir announced that the science lab would stay locked after three o'clock, even for students preparing the fair project. Twelve students went quiet. Irfan stood up. "Sir, I get why there is a rule, but I cannot see how it is fair for the fair teams. Can we talk about it?" Someone giggled nervously. Meena stared at her desk, and Ravi shook his head. Gautam Sir raised an eyebrow, then folded his arms. "Meet me after class. Bring your idea." Irfan sat down; his hands were cold, but his voice had stayed steady.

qa.q: After what time would the science lab stay locked?
qa.a: The science lab would stay locked after three o'clock.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel while standing up to speak?
qa.a: Irfan felt nervous, with cold hands, yet steady enough to speak; he was afraid of the reaction but wanted to be fair to the fair teams.

qa.q: What made Irfan's disagreement work?
qa.a: Irfan first accepted that a rule can have a reason and then asked to talk, which separated respect for the teacher from agreement with the order.

qa.q: How might Gautam Sir have felt on hearing Irfan?
qa.a: Gautam Sir may have been surprised, given the raised eyebrow and folded arms, but he was open enough to invite Irfan to meet after class with an idea.

grounding: A teenager says I understand the rule but do not think it is fair, and asks to discuss it, separating respect from agreement.

passage: In a Manchester school, Mr Kofi handed Chen a detention slip for arriving late. Chen looked at it, took a breath and said, "I understand there is a rule about lateness, but the bus was cancelled and I do not think detention is fair. Could we talk after class?" Two classmates behind exchanged glances. Priya smiled at her shoes. Mr Kofi's mouth tightened. "After class, then." At the end of the lesson Chen showed the bus notice on a phone. Mr Kofi read it, nodded slowly, and tore up the slip.

qa.q: What did Chen show Mr Kofi at the end of the lesson?
qa.a: Chen showed the bus notice on a phone.

qa.q: What was Mr Kofi feeling when his mouth tightened?
qa.a: Mr Kofi was probably irritated or challenged at being questioned in front of the class, though he still agreed to talk afterwards.

qa.q: What in Chen's wording kept the disagreement respectful?
qa.a: Chen began with "I understand there is a rule", gave a reason, and asked to talk after class instead of arguing in front of everyone.

qa.q: What might Priya be feeling while smiling at her shoes?
qa.a: Priya may feel nervous and quietly impressed, or relieved that someone said it out loud; looking at her shoes suggests not wanting to be seen reacting.

grounding: A teenager says I understand the rule, but I do not think this is fair, and asks to discuss it, separating respect from agreement.
